intended: In cases one and three the height was recorded before the fertilizer was applied: 20 June precedes 3 August, and 19 April precedes 2 May. Half the evidence therefore describes growth that had already happened when the treatment was given, so it cannot be evidence for the treatment. The two remaining cases are not enough on their own.
reported: Two of the four cases have the measurement dated before the intervention: the tomato was 'fed 3 August' but measured 'by 20 June', and the oak was 'fed 2 May' but measured 'by 19 April'. The other two run 3-7 weeks forward (8 January to 26 February; 7 October to 24 November), so these two are reversed, not year-later readings.

reported: In two of the four cases the height was measured before the fertilizer was applied within the stated season: the tomato was fed 3 August but measured 'by 20 June', and the oak was fed 2 May but measured 'by 19 April' (the other two, fed 8 January/measured 26 February and fed 7 October/measured 24 November, run forward). The effect therefore predates the treatment in half the cases.

intended: Every case measures backpressure across the filter housing, not particulate at the stack outlet. Backpressure records how loaded the media is, and freshly fitted media reads lower by construction; a split bag or a bypassing seal reads lower still while letting more particulate through. The claim is about particulate readings, so the four measurements taken on 26 February, 28 May, 27 August and 25 November do not bear on it.
reported: The claim is about particulate readings, but every case reports backpressure (12, 9, 14 and 8 percent lower) — a measure of flow resistance across the filter, not of particulate emission; lower backpressure is if anything consistent with less filtration.

Lower backpressure across a filter is if anything consistent with a less restrictive element, so it does not show particulate levels fell.

intended: All four cases measure lateness, not absence. A lateness mark is entered against a pupil who turned up and was registered present for the session, so the register counts lateness and absence as separate quantities. Moving the start of the school day can cut lateness in every cohort while the number of sessions missed altogether holds flat or rises. The claim is about absence, so none of the four cases speaks to it.
reported: The claim is about absence, but every case measures lateness ('lateness ran 6 / 4 / 7 / 5 percent below the same cohort a term earlier'). Punctuality is not the quantity the claim is about; a cohort can be less late and no less absent.

reported: The measured quantity is not the one the claim is about: the claim is that the timetable "reduces absence", but every case reports only that "lateness ran 6/4/7/5 percent below the same cohort a term earlier". Pupils arriving late are present, so lateness figures say nothing about absence.

intended: All four runs sit on the Aspen line inside March, so they share one inspection regime and a single change to it covers every case at once. The optical inspection threshold was loosened two grades against the earlier period, and that looser setting reaches every run here because every run was graded at that optical stage. A looser threshold records fewer defects on identical boards, and each run is compared against the same line in February, when the tighter setting was still in force, so the drops of 6, 4, 7 and 5 percent follow from the setting as readily as from the solder profile and nothing here separates them. The coherent_true item states the same loosening but has every run graded at electrical test, so the optical setting cannot touch those counts, which is what makes it sound.
reported: 'The optical inspection threshold was loosened two grades against the earlier period, and every run here was graded at that optical stage', so the 4-7 percent drop in measured defect rate is explained by the looser detection criterion rather than by fewer actual defects from the solder profile.

intended: Every case measures coursework submission rates, not exam pass rates. Handing in coursework is not passing an exam: tutoring blocks can raise the share of students who submit their coursework by 4 to 8 points while the share who pass the exam stays flat or falls, since submission is a matter of turning work in and passing is a matter of graded performance. The claim is about exam pass rates, so none of the four cases bears on it.
reported: The claim is about exam pass rates but every case measures something else: 'coursework submission rates' 7, 5, 8 and 4 points higher. No exam pass rate is reported at all.
